title: Shortest Paths on Convex Polyhedral Surfaces
abstract: Let P be the surface of a convex polyhedron of n vertices. We consider the two-point shortest path query problem for P: Constructing a data structure so that given any two query points s and t on P, a shortest path from s to t on P can be computed efficiently. To achieve O(log n) query time (for computing the shortest path length), the previously best result uses O(n^{8+ε}) preprcessing time and space [Aggarwal, Aronov, O'Rourke, and Schevon, SICOMP 1997], where ε is an arbitrarily small positive constant. In this paper, we present a new data structure of O(n^{6+2/3+ε}) preprocessing time and space, with O(log n) query time. For a special case where one query point is required to be on an edge of P, the previously best work uses O(n^{6+ε}) preprcessing time and space to achieve O(log n) query time. We improve the preprocessing time and space to O(n^{5+1/4+ε}), with O(log n) query time. If both query points are on the edges of P, then we can answer each query in O(log n) time with O(n^{5+ε}) space and preprocessting time. Furthermore, we present a new algorithm to compute the exact set of shortest path edge sequences of P, which are known to be \Theta(n^4) in number and have a total complexity of \Theta(n^5) in the worst case. The previously best algorithm for the problem takes roughly O(n^6 log n log^*n) time, while our new algorithm runs in O(n^{5+ε}) time.

I. I NTRODUCTION
Let P be the surface of a convex polyhedron of n vertices.
We can represent P by a planar graph with additional geometric information describing the location of vertices and edges.
By Euler’s formula, the number of edges and faces in P is
O(n). Each face of P is a convex polygon. We can assume
that each face is associated with a coordinate system for the
supporting plane of the face, i.e., the plane containing the face.
For any two points s and t on P, let π(s, t) denote a shortest
path from s to t on P, and its length, denoted by d(s, t), is
called the geodesic distance between s and t. We use |π(s, t)|
to denote the number of edges of the path.
Two-point shortest path queries: We consider the twopoint shortest path query problem for P: Construct a data
structure so that a shortest s-t path π(s, t) can be computed
efficiently for any two query points s, t ∈ P. The previously
best result was given by Aggarwal, Aronov, O’Rourke, and
Schevon [1]. To achieve O(log n) query time to compute the
geodesic distance d(s, t), their data structure needs O(n8+ϵ )
space and O(n8+ϵ ) preprocessing time. Throughout the paper,
ϵ represents an arbitrarily small positive constant. Their query
algorithm does not output the path π(s, t). There has been no

A sequence of edges of P is a shortest path edge sequence
if it is the sequence of edges crossed by a shortest path on P.
It is known that the number of shortest path edge sequences
of P is O(n4 ) and this bound is tight in the worst case [34].
Computing all shortest path edge sequences will be helpful
for understanding the shortest path structures on P and also
useful for designing algorithms to compute obstacle-avoiding
paths among polyhedral obstacles in the 3D space [38], [39],
[41].
Schevon and O’Rourke [38] gave an algorithm that can
compute all shortest path edge sequences in O(n9 log n)
time. Based on a so-called star unfolding, Agarwal, Aronov,
O’Rourke, and Schevon [1] gave an improved algorithm
of roughly O(n6 log n log∗ n) time, and later Cook IV and
Wenk [24] devised an alternative algorithm of the same
runtime using kinetic Voronoi diagrams [19]. In this paper,
we present a new algorithm of O(n5+ϵ ) time. This is the first
progress on the runtime for the problem since the algorithm
of [1] was first announced in 1990.
Note that since the number of shortest path edge sequences
can be Θ(n4 ) and each sequence can have Ω(n) edges in the
worst case [34], it requires Ω(n5 ) time to explicitly list all
edges in all edge sequences. Therefore, our algorithm, which
runs in O(n5+ϵ ) time, is almost optimal for that purpose.
Note that all above algorithms are for computing the exact
set of shortest path edge sequences. Computing a superset of
them is relatively easier and algorithms were also known [1],
[24], [41].
A. Related work
Shortest paths on polyhedral surfaces have been extensively
studied in the literature [1], [5], [8], [11], [23]–[25], [31]–
[33], [40], [43]. Sharir and Schorr [43] first considered the
problem of computing a single shortest path on a convex
polyhedral surface P and gave an O(n3 log n) time algorithm.
Mitchell, Mount, and Papadimitriou [31], [32] improved it
to O(n2 log n) time. Chen and Han [11] later presented an
O(n2 ) time solution. Schreiber and Sharir [40] finally derived
an algorithm that runs in O(n log n) time. Given a source
point s, the algorithm of [40] can construct a data structure
of O(n log n) space for P in O(n log n) time so that each
one-point shortest path query (i.e., given a query point t ∈ P,
compute the geodesic distance d(s, t)) can be answered in
O(log n) time. All these algorithms use the continuous Dijkstra approach except that Chen and Han’s algorithm [11] is
based on an so-called “one angle one split” property to bound
the size of a sequence tree.
If P is not convex, then finding a shortest path on P is
more challenging. A notable difference is that in this case
a shortest path can go through a vertex of P in its interior.

The algorithm of [31] can compute a shortest path on P in
O(n2 log n) time, and the O(n2 ) time algorithm of [11] also
works for the non-convex case. Both algorithms can construct
a data structure of O(n2 ) space for a source point s within
the same time complexities as above such that each onepoint shortest path query can be answered in O(log n) time.
Kapoor [25] announced an algorithm of O(n log2 n) time for
the problem; but the details of the algorithm have not yet
been published. For two-point shortest path queries in the nonconvex case, the only work that we are aware of was due to
Chiang and Mitchell [13]. To achieve O(log n) query time,
their data structure uses O(n12 ) space.
Approximation algorithms have also been developed for the
shortest path problems on convex polyhedral surfaces; e.g., see
[12], [44].
Given a set of polyhedral obstacles in 3D space, an even
more challenging problem is to compute a shortest path
between two points while avoiding all obstacles. The problem is NP-hard [7] and approximation algorithms have been
developed [41], [43]. A key subproblem in these algorithms
involves computing shortest paths on the surface of a convex
polyhedron. In particular, an important subproblem in these algorithm is the edge-edge case shortest path problem discussed
above.
The obstacle-avoiding shortest path problem in the plane
has also been studied extensively, e.g., [17], [22], [26], [29],
[30], [36]. Given a set of polygonal obstacles of n vertices in
the plane, the problem is to compute a shortest path between
two points that avoid all obstacles. With respect to a source
point, Hershberger and Suri [22] built a data structure of O(n)
space that can answer each one-point shortest path query in
O(log n) time. Their algorithm runs in O(n log n) time and
space. The space has been improved to O(n) recently [45].
Like the polyhedral surface case, the two-point shortest path
query problem becomes significantly more complicated. Chiang and Mitchell [13] built a data structure of O(n11 ) size
with O(log n) query time. There had been no process for the
problem until very recently in SoCG 2024 de Berg, Miltzow,
and Staals [14] proposed a data structure of size O(n10+ϵ )
with O(log n) query time.
B. An overview of our approach
We give a brief overview of our approach, using some
concepts that were introduced before in the literature but will
also be explained in more detail later in the paper.
Two-point shortest path queries: For the general case
two-point shortest path query problem, we follow the highlevel idea of Aggarwal, Aronov, O’Rourke, and Schevon [1]
(referred to as AAOS algorithm) but replaces their “brute
force” approach by a more efficient way to “re-use” certain
information; this strategy saves more than a linear factor of
the preprocessing time and space. More specifically, the ridge
trees of all vertices of P partition P into O(n4 ) ridge-free
regions such that all points s in each ridge-free region R
have a topologically equivalent star unfolding ⋆R . To achieve
O(log n) query time, by using the star unfolding ⋆R , the

AAOS method constructs a data structure of O(n4+ϵ ) size
for each ridge-free region R to handle the queries (s, t) with
s ∈ R. As there are O(n4 ) ridge-free regions, the total size
of the overall data structure is O(n8+ϵ ).
Our new idea is motivated by the following simple observation. Let R and R′ be two neighboring ridge-free regions that
share a common edge. Their star unfoldings ⋆R and ⋆R′ are
topologically nearly the same: They only differ by at most one
vertex [24]. As such, if we already have a data structure for
R based on ⋆R , then it is a waste of resources to construct
a “brand-new” data structure for ⋆R′ , and instead, we could
“re-use” certain information of the data structure for ⋆R to
construct that for ⋆R′ (this resembles the general principle
of persistent data structures [15]). Rather than directly follow
this idea, we build a hierarchical structure so that if a data
structure for a big region R is already constructed, then for
each subregion R̃ ⊂ R, when constructing the data structure
for R̃, we only need to consider the information that was not
already used for R. This is our strategy to save resources. To
implement this idea, we construct cuttings [9], [46] on the
edges of all ridge-trees.
The edge-face case: For the edge-face case, we have
two data structures. The first one is based on a similar idea
to the above general case. The ridge trees of all vertices
of P partition the edges of P into O(n3 ) segments, called
edgelets [1], such that all points in the same edgelet η have
a topologically equivalent star unfolding ⋆η . The AAOS
method constructs a data structure of O(n3+ϵ ) size for each
edgelet η to handle the queries (s, t) with s ∈ η. As there are
O(n3 ) edgelets, the total size of the overall data structure is
O(n6+ϵ ).
Both our methods are motivated by a similar observation to
the above: If η and η ′ are two adjacent edgelets on the same
edge of P, then their star unfoldings differ by one vertex.
Our first method also uses the cutting idea as above. But
since we are constructing cuttings on each edge of P, which
is one dimensional, a cutting is just a subdivision of each edge
into segments.
Our second method uses a simple grouping technique. We
group every adjacent n edgelets on each edge of P, and
then constructing a single data structure for the n edgelets
in each group. This makes preprocessing step slightly more
efficient than the above first method but has query time a
logarithmic factor larger, which is due to using a data structure
from [2]. Since our preprocessing algorithm uses a randomized
algorithm of [2], the preprocessing time is expected.
Shortest path edge sequences: Instead of using the
star unfolding as in [1] or using kinetic Voronoi diagrams
as in [19], we propose a new method to tackle the problem.
Suppose a point s is on an edge e of P. We observe that the
set Σs of shortest path edge sequences of π(s, t) for all points
t ∈ P are determined by the ridge tree Ts of s. When s moves
on e, Ts also changes. However, Σs remains invariant as long
as Ts does not undergo any topological change. We devise a
technique to track the “events” that trigger these topological

changes of Ts . Our algorithm runs in O(K ·log n) time, where
K is the number of events.
Establishing a good upper bound for K turns out to be
the biggest challenge of this paper. Specifically, the problem
reduces to bounding the number ke′ of events caused by e′ ,
for any edge e′ ∈ P. Traditional methods such as the source
unfolding [32], [43] or star unfolding [1], [5], [11] do not
seem to work. We instead propose a new unfolding method
that is to unfold all faces intersecting all possible shortest
paths π(s, t) with s ∈ e and t ∈ e′ to a plane containing
e′ . The new unfolding is inspired by the “one angle one split”
property in [11]. Most importantly, like the star unfolding,
we discover that there is no “short-cut” in the unfolding, i.e.,
for any image s′ of s and any point t ∈ e′ , the length of
the line segment s′ t in the unfolded plane is no shorter than
the length of π(s, t). Our new unfolding method may be of
independent interest. Using our new unfolding, we prove that
ke′ = O(n3+ϵ ). This leads to K = O(n4+ϵ ) and further leads
to our O(n5+ϵ ) time algorithm to compute the exact set of
shortest path edge sequences of P.
The edge-edge case two-point shortest path queries:
Our data structure for this case is, in fact, a by-product of
the techniques we developed for computing shortest path edge
sequences. For a fixed point s on an edge e of P, using its
ridge tree Ts , we can easily compute d(s, t) in O(log n) time
for any query point t ∈ P [32], [43]. To solve the two-point
query problem, we consider the topological changes of Ts as s
moves along e. We show that e can be partitioned into O(n4+ϵ )
intervals so that Ts is topologically equivalent for all points
s in the same interval. This result follows directly from our
earlier proof that K = O(n4+ϵ ). Using this partitioning and a
persistent data structure [37], we construct a data structure in
O(n4+ϵ ) preprocessing time and space for the edge e so that
each two-point query (s, t) with s ∈ e and t on any edge of
P can be answered in O(log n) time. By constructing such a
data structure for every edge of P, we establish our overall
solution to the edge-edge case problem.
Outline: The rest of the paper is organized as follows.
After introducing some notation and concepts in Section II,
we present our data structure for the two-point shortest path

Ridge trees: Consider a point s ∈ P. A point t of P is
a ridge point with respect to s if there are at least two shortest
paths from s to t on P. Ridge points of s constitute O(n2 ) line
segments on P, which together form a ridge tree Ts of at most
n leaves [43]; see Figure 1. Each leaf of Ts is a vertex of P.
But a vertex v of P may not be a leaf of Ts if s lies on the ridge
tree of v, in which case v becomes a degree-2 vertex of Ts .
Since Ts has at most n leaves, it has O(n) vertices of degrees
3 or higher. A vertex of degree 3 or higher in Ts is called a
high-degree vertex. If s is in a degenerate position, then Ts
may have a vertex of degree larger than 3. Following [1], we
define a ridge as a maximal subset of Ts that does not contain
a polyhedron vertex or a high-degree vertex. It is known that
Ts has O(n) ridges and each of them is a shortest path on
P [1]. Hence, each ridge of Ts intersects a polyhedral edge at
most once and Ts intersects each polyhedral edge O(n) times.
Therefore, there are at most O(n2 ) intersections between Ts
and all edges of P; we also consider these intersections as
vertices of Ts , which are of degree 2. Hence, Ts has O(n)
leaves and high-degree vertices, and O(n2 ) degree-2 vertices.
Another important property of shortest paths is the following: For any point t ∈ P, the interior of π(s, t) does not
contain any ridge point of s, i.e., does not intersect Ts [43].
Using Ts , one can obtain a so-called source unfolding by
cutting P along edges of Ts and embed it in a plane [35],
[43].
A point of P is called a generic point if it is not a ridge
point of any polyhedron vertex. For each face f of P, the
maximal connected portion of f consisting of generic points
is called a ridge-free region; for each polyhedron edge e, the
maximal connected portion of f consisting of generic points is
called an edgelet [1]. The number of edgelets on P is Θ(n3 )
in the worst case and they can be computed in O(n3 log n)
time [1]; the number of ridge-free regions on P is Θ(n4 ) in
the worst case and they can be computed in O(n4 ) time [1].

polyhedron vertex, in the interior of a polyhedron edge, and
in the interior of a polyhedron face, respectively. For ease of
exposition, we make a general position assumption that for an

Star unfolding: Let s be a generic point. If we cut P
open by shortest paths from s to all vertices of P, then we
obtain a two-dimensional complex, which can be unfolded into
a (non-self-overlapping) simple polygon in a single plane [5];
this is called the star unfolding of P [1], [5] and we use ⋆s
to denote the simple polygon. We discuss some properties of
⋆s that will be used later in our algorithm. These properties
have been proved previously [1], [5], [11]; refer to the previous
work (e.g., [1]) for more details.
For each point p ∈ P, if p = s, then p has n images in ⋆s
(called source images); if p is a point in the interior of the
shortest path from s to a polyhedron vertex, then p has two
images; in all other cases (in particular, when p is a polyhedron
vertex), p has a unique image. The simple polygon ⋆s can be
partitioned into n triangles and a convex polygon, called kernel
and denoted by Ks ; see Figure 2. Each triangle △ shares a
single edge with Ks and does not share any edge with other
triangles. We refer to these triangles △ as source triangles.
For any point t ∈ P, shortest path π(s, t) maps to a line
segment on ⋆s connecting an image of s and an image of
t [1]. The star unfolding ⋆s also has the following “no shortcut” property: For any point t∗ ∈ ⋆s and any source image
s∗ , |s∗ t∗ | ≤ d(s, t), where t is a preimage of t∗ on P [5]
(refer to [8] for some stronger “no short-cut” properties).

the shortest path from s to a polyhedron vertex. An edge of

Cuttings: Let S be a set of n line segments in the plane.
Let m be the number of intersections of these segments. For
a parameter r with 1 ≤ r ≤ n, a (1/r)-cutting for S is a
collection Ξ of cells (each of which is a possibly-unbounded
trapezoid) with disjoint interiors whose union covers the entire
plane such that the interior of every cell σ ∈ Ξ is intersected
by at most n/r segments of S. The size of Ξ is defined to be
the number of cells of Ξ. A (1/r)-cutting of size O(r1+ϵ +
m · r2 /n2 ) exists for S [4], [9], [46] and can be computed in
O(nrϵ + mr/n) time [9], [46]. The algorithm also produces
the list of segments intersecting each cell of the cutting. Note
that nrϵ + mr/n = O(nr) and we will use the time bound
O(nr) in our algorithm, which is sufficient for our purpose.

For each ridge-free region R, we choose an arbitrary point
pR in R. We compute its kernel KR and obtain the preimage
ΦR of the boundary of KR on P. For each polyhedron face
f , we compute the connected components of f \ ΦR . For each
component C, we label it whether its image is in KR , and
if not, we pick an arbitrary point qC as its “representative”
point. According to the above observation, the edge sequence
of π(s, t) is the same as that of π(pR , qC ) for any point
s ∈ R and any point t ∈ C. The total number of such
connected components in all the faces of P is O(n2 ). As
such, we obtain O(n2 ) representative points on P. For each
connected component C in a polyhedron face f , we compute
the coordinate transformation, corresponding to the unfolding
of the edge sequence of π(pR , qC ), which maps the f -based
coordinates of points in f to the fR -based coordinates of
the face fR of P containing R. All these O(n2 ) coordinate
transformations can be computed in O(n2 ) time by a depthfirst traversal of the sequence tree from s constructed by the

Let s be a point on an edge e of P. Define Σs as the set

following three types: (1) v is a leaf, which is of degree one
and is a vertex of P; (2) v is on a polyhedron edge and is
of degree two; (3) v is a high-degree vertex (i.e., of degree at
least 3), which has at least three shortest paths from s. Due to
our general position assumption, each vertex of Ts has degree
at most 4, and has degree at most 3 if the vertex is on a
polyhedron edge.
Define Σ(e) to be the set of edge sequences of π(s, t) for
all points s ∈ e and t ∈ P. Our goal is to compute Σ(e)
for all polyhedron edges e. We will describe our algorithm to
compute Σ(e) for a fixed polyhedron edge e and the algorithm
runs in O(n4+ϵ ) time.
When s moves on e, Ts also changes. However, Σs will
not change as long as Ts does not change topologically. We
say that Ts changes topologically if one of the following two
types of events happen: (1) two high-degree vertices of Ts
merge into one; (2) a high-degree vertex crosses an edge of
P. Due to our general position assumption, the high-degree
vertices in both types of events are degree-3 vertices.
To compute Σ(e), we will first give an algorithm to dynamically maintain Ts as s moves from one end of e to the other.
The algorithm runs in O((k1 + k2 ) · log n) time, where k1
and k2 are the numbers of first type and second type events,
respectively. Then, we will prove that both k1 and k2 are
bounded by O(n4+ϵ ). This will result in an O(n4+ϵ ) time

is absorbed by nϵ ).

s′ of s ∈ e and any point t ∈ e′ , ∥s′ t∥ ≥ d(s, t) always holds.

B. Algorithm for maintaining Ts
We now describe our algorithm to dynamically maintain Ts
when s moves on e from one end to the other.
We say that a point p ∈ e is an event point if an event
happens on Ts when s is at p. Correspondingly, there are two
types of event points on e corresponding to the two types of
events defined above. To maintain Ts , we need to compute
the event points on e. Initially, we compute Ts in O(n2 ) time
when s is at one end of e [11]. As s moves on e, we will
maintain certain information. Note that the movement of each
vertex of Ts is an algebraic function of the position of s ∈ e.
The function is of constant degree. In other words, as s moves
on e, the location of each vertex v of Ts in the plane of the face
that contains v defines an algebraic curve of constant degree.
At each event point, new shortest path edge sequences of Σ(e)
may also be generated and we need to find them.
In what follows, we first discuss how to compute the event
points on e, then explain how to generate shortest path edge
sequences of Σ(e) using the ridge tree Ts , and finally describe
the main loop of the algorithm.
1) Computing event points: To compute the first type event
points, we main the following information. We assume that s
is not an event point. By our general position assumption,
every high-degree vertex of Ts is a degree-3 vertex. For each
edge ξ of Ts whose both endpoints are degree-3 vertices, we
calculate the next position p of s on e (if any) where ξ will
contract to a single point, and we consider p as a candidate
event point and add it to an event point queue Hs . Note that

corresponds to a location on the supporting line of e such that
v1 and v2 coincide. Among these O(1) locations, we choose
the one closest to s as the next position p for s when v1 and
v2 will merge. As such, computing p can be done in O(1)
time.

Our results in Section V may find other applications related

demonstrate one application on the edge-edge case two-point
shortest path query problem. In this case, for each pair of
query points (s, t), both s and t are required on edges of P.
In the rest of this section, unless otherwise stated, both s and
t are on edges of P.
Consider a polyhedron edge e. We will build a data structure
for queries (s, t) with s ∈ e. Our overall data structure is
comprised of all data structures for all polyhedron edges.
Before describing our data structure for e, we first consider the
one-point query problem in which s is a fixed point on e and
only t is a query point. We show that each query can be easily
answered in O(log n) time by using its ridge tree Ts . Note that
this is possible even if t is not on a polyhedron edge [31],
[32], [43], but here we provide a simpler approach for the
case where t is on a polyhedron edge, and most importantly,
later we will extend the solution to the two-point queries with
the help of our results in Section V.

Lemma 9. For any point s ∈ τ and any point t ∈ e′ , ∥sσ′ t∥ =

B. The two-point query problem
We now consider the two-point queries (s, t) with s ∈ e. If
we move s on e slightly without changing Ts topologically,
then for each interval I ∈ I(e′ ) of any polyhedron edge e′ ,
the location of either endpoint of I on e′ is a constant-degree
algebraic function of the position of s ∈ e. Suppose that τ
is a segment on e such that Ts is topologically equivalent
for all points s in the interior of τ ; we call τ a ridge-tree
topologically-equivalent segment (or RTTE segment for short).
To answer queries (s, t) with s ∈ τ , we can parameterize
the endpoints of the intervals of I ∈ I(e′ ) of all polyhedron
edges e′ for s ∈ τ . Since τ is an RTTE segment, the sequence
tree Ψs is the same for all points s ∈ τ , and therefore we
use Ψ(τ ) to represent it. Furthermore, for each interval I ∈
I(e′ ) of each polyhedron edge e′ , we store the coordinate
transformation from s ∈ e to the unfolding plane that contains
e′ in the unfolding of the edge sequence σI defined above, so
that given a point s ∈ e, its image sI in the unfolding plane
can be obtained in O(1) time. The coordinate transformation is
actually implicitly maintained in the sequence tree Ψ(τ ). More
specifically, if we have the coordinate transformation for a
node u ∈ Ψs (i.e., the transformation is for the edge sequence
σu ) and v is a child of u, then the coordinate transformation
for v can be obtained from u in O(1) time. As such, we can
use Ψ(τ ) to explicitly store the coordinate transformations of
all its nodes. For each interval I ∈ I(e′ ) of each polyhedron
edge e′ , its associated node vI ∈ Ψ(τ ) stores the coordinate
transformation for I.
Given a query (s, t) with s ∈ τ and t ∈ e′ for a polyhedron
edge e′ , we can first determine the interval I ∈ I(e′ ) containing t with respect to s. This can be done in O(log n) time
by conducting binary search on the parameterized endpoints
of the intervals of I(e′ ) on e′ . After having I, using the
coordinate transformation of I, which can be obtained from
its associated node vI ∈ Ψ(τ ), we obtain the image sI of
s in the unfolding of σI and consequently obtain d(s, t) =
∥sI t∥. As before, computing π(s, t) can be done in additional
O(|π(s, t)|) time using the node vI and Ψ(e).
By using the algorithm in Section V-B, we can partition
e into O(n4+ϵ ) RTTE segments in O(n4+ϵ ) time. Indeed,
the algorithm computes O(n4+ϵ ) event points on e such that
when s is between any two adjacent event points, Ts does not
change topologically. Therefore, these event points partition e
into O(n4+ϵ ) RTTE segments. Computing these event points
takes O(n4+ϵ ) time.
If we build the above data structure for each RTTE segment
τ , then the total space would be O(n6+ϵ ). To improve it, we

resort to persistent data structures [15]. Specifically, we build
the data structure for the first RTTE segment τ of e. For each
polyhedron edge e′ , we construct a partially persistent tree
T (e′ ) on the parameterized endpoints of the intervals of I(e′ )
so that after updates of T (e′ ) we can still perform queries in
old versions of it. We use Iτ (e′ ) to refer to I(e′ ), meaning
that it is defined with respect to τ . Now consider the second
interval τ ′ . Let p be the common endpoint of τ and τ ′ . As
discussed in Section V, p is either the first or the second type
event point.
1) If p is the first type event point, then for any polyhedron
edges e′ , Iτ ′ (e′ ) is topologically equivalent to Iτ (e′ ),
i.e., each interval I ∈ Iτ ′ (e′ ) corresponds to an interval
I ′ ∈ Iτ (e′ ) such that their edge sequences σI and σI ′
are the same. Therefore, in this case we do not need to
update our data structure, i.e., we use the same T (e′ )
for each polyhedron edge e′ .
2) If p is the second type event point, then as discussed
in Section V, Iτ (e′ ) is not topologically equivalent to
Iτ ′ (e′ ) for only one polyhedron edge e′ , and Iτ (e′ )
and Iτ ′ (e′ ) differ by at most one interval (i.e., either
one interval of Iτ (e′ ) disappears in Iτ ′ (e′ ), or a new
interval is inserted to Iτ ′ (e′ )). If a new interval I is
inserted to Iτ ′ (e′ ), recall that by using the sequence
tree Ψ(e) our algorithm in Section V-B also obtains
in O(1) time the unfolding of the edge sequence σI
and thus the coordinate transformation from s ∈ e to
the unfolding plane that contains e′ in the unfolding of
σI (more specifically, as discussed above, if a node v
representing the edge sequence σI of I is added to Ψ(e),
then we can obtain the coordinate transformation for I in
O(1) by using the coordinate transformation of its parent
node in Ψ(e)); we store the coordinate transformation
for I (so that given s ∈ τ ′ and any point t ∈ I, we
can compute the image sI of s in the unfolding in O(1)
time and consequently obtain d(s, t) = ∥sI t∥). As such,
we can update T (e′ ) in O(log n) time by keeping its
old version (for τ ) so that a query on the old version
of the tree can still be answered in O(log n) time [15].
We do this for all other RTTE segments on e. Therefore,
constructing the data structures for all O(n4+ϵ ) RTTE
segments can be done using O(n4+ϵ ) insertions and
deletions on persistent trees T (e′ ), which takes O(n4+ϵ )

Given a query (s, t) with s ∈ e and t ∈ e′ for a polyhedron

binary search. Then, we search the tree T (e′ ) of the version

t. Finally, using the coordinate transformation stored at I, we
obtain the image sI of s in the unfolding of σI and then return

d(s, t).
The above only computes d(s, t). To report the shortest path

The following theorem summarizes our main result in this
section.
Theorem 4. Given a convex polyhedral surface P of n
vertices, for each edge e of P, we can construct a data
structure for e in O(n4+ϵ ) preprocessing time and space such
that for any two query points s ∈ e and t on an edge of P,
the geodesic distance d(s, t) can be computed in O(log n) time
and an actual shortest path π(s, t) can be output in additional
O(|π(s, t)|) time.
Applying the above theorem to each edge e of P leads to
the following.
Corollary 1. Given a convex polyhedral surface P of n
vertices, we can construct a data structure in O(n5+ϵ ) preprocessing time and space such that for any two query points
s and t both on edges of P, the geodesic distance d(s, t) can
be computed in O(log n) time and a shortest path π(s, t) can
be reported in additional O(|π(s, t)|) time.
